rv.q: Lloyd Webber's score sounds great... Fendall's work is wonderful, including costumes and wigs that play attractive games with a gamut of textures.
McOnie clearly loves Cats but this production often doesn't feel very catty.
Really it’s a very decent production of a tuneful and idiosyncratic musical that just happens to have sold a kerchillion tickets back in the day.
It works best as a showcase for the energetic young cast and what it does best – which is dance.
Fendall's costuming alone is worth making the trek for.
The oddest musical works its magic again.
McOnie makes half a case for it with this hit-and-miss revival but doesn’t quite reach the Heaviside Layer before daybreak.
Even by musical theatre standards, the show is sluggish and too repetitive.

What Drew McOnie has created with this production is nothing short of sensational - truly awe-inspiring and a show that has just established himself as the front-runner to sweep the Olivier Awards next year.
Overall, this is probably one of my favourite productions which the Regent's Air Theatre has staged over the last few years.
There's not a dustbin in sight in director and choreographer Drew McOnie's sexed up, high-octane production that stirs and transfixes.
Melanie La Barrie also proves she can lead a cast as Old Deuteronomy who is ringleader for the only real plot you need to know.
Few musicals give movement, imagination and theatrical playfulness quite so much room to take over.
For those seeking a nostalgic return to one of musical theatre's most distinctive creations, this revival offers plenty of entertainment, even if it occasionally falls short of its full potential.
The first half, however, needs greater energy, spectacle, individuality and visual clarity.

cn.t: Drew McOnie's outdoor revival earns mostly positive reviews for its contemporary choreography and strong performances, though critics note the show's inherently loose narrative remains divisive for those unfamiliar with its peculiar charms.
